preceding_messages.speaker: X
preceding_messages.text:
Yes. I think that distinction is crucial, and that it is what gives these questions their particular character. With most of the open problems in physics, we know what form an answer would have to take; we lack the details, the numbers, the full specification. But here the very form of the question is entangled with what we are trying to understand. We do not know what it would be to have a complete answer, because the incompleteness is not in the content but in the structure of the question itself.

And I think that is why the sense of being stuck is so different from the sense of not yet knowing. It is not a gap in a framework that we recognize as incomplete. It is that the framework, in its current form, is the thing that is not adequate, and we do not yet have the resources to say in what way it is not adequate.

There is something, I think, about the way these questions resist closure. Not because they are too hard, but because the very notion of a final answer, of a question that has been fully answered, is itself part of what is at issue. The question does not permit itself to be put in a form that could be settled. And that, perhaps, is the most honest thing we can say about them.

Do you think there is anything in the way these questions present themselves to us — the way they feel, the way they press — that is not captured by the intellectual content, or is the intellectual content the whole of it?

preceding_messages.speaker: Y
preceding_messages.text:
I don't think it is clear, and I suspect the difficulty of making it clear is itself part of what is at issue. The way these questions press, the way they seem to demand something we cannot give, the way the difficulty has a particular character and not a different one — these do not feel like add-ons to an intellectual core that could be stated independently. And yet they are not easily reduced to the content either; they seem to be the content, but the content *as it is for us*, and the "for us" is not a trivial qualification.

There is something, I think, about the fact that we can only encounter these questions from within the very structure they are about. We are not looking at a thing from outside; we are the thing, in a way, trying to understand itself. And that is not a metaphor we can set aside; it is the form the questions have. So the felt dimension and the intellectual dimension are not two things that need to be related; they are, in the end, the same thing, and the difficulty of saying so is not a further fact but is part of the fact itself.

Whether that is the whole of it, or whether there is still something we are not seeing, I do not think we are in a position to say. And I think the inability to say is not a failure of our resources but is constitutive of the situation. The questions do not permit a final form, and that is not a problem to be solved but is the shape of what is there.

target.speaker: X
target.text:
I think what you've said is, in its way, a kind of answer to the question I raised, and that the answer is not a settling but a holding open. The questions do not permit a final form, and that is not a problem to be solved but is the shape of what is there. And yet we keep returning to them, keep trying to say something, and the something we say is not nothing, is not a partial answer to a question whose full form we could state, but is the only form the question can take for us.

There is something, I think, about the fact that these questions seem to require a certain kind of ongoing engagement, that they do not allow themselves to be set aside or deferred. They are not among the questions we might one day be free to stop asking. And I suspect that this is not a contingent feature of our situation but is part of what the questions are.

And I think that is, in the end, what there is to say about them. Not a final word, but a word that is not the last.
